result.summary: Orpheus sits on a bare, shadeless hill and plays his lyre. Trees of every kind come to gather around him and make shade. The pine is named last, as the tree into which Attis was changed.

scenes.title: Orpheus summons the trees
scenes.summary: On a treeless grassy hill Orpheus plays, and a long catalogue of trees arrives to shade him. The passage ends with the pine, tied to the transformation of Attis.

characters.name: Orpheus

characters.name: Attis
characters.description: follower of the Mother of the Gods, turned into a pine

characters.name: Mother of the Gods
characters.description: Cybele, who loves the pine tree

notable_quotes.reason: Orpheus's music is so powerful that it creates shade where there was none.

analysis.text: The power of song over nature is shown through trees that move to listen. The passage also links Orpheus's tale to another metamorphosis, that of Attis.
Ovid's long catalogue of trees follows an epic tradition of lists, and displays his knowledge of Roman botany and cult.

legacy.text: The image of Orpheus moving trees and beasts with music became a standard emblem of art's power in Renaissance poetry and opera.

fun_facts.text: The pine was sacred to Cybele, and in her Roman cult a pine tree was carried in procession in spring.

language_notes.text: The tree of Chaonia is the oak, sacred to Jupiter at Dodona in Chaonia (Epirus), whose oracle spoke through its rustling leaves.
The grove of the Heliades means poplars, or alders in some versions: the sisters of Phaethon, mourning him, were turned into trees whose tears became amber.
Mast-tree means a tall tree used for ship masts, here the fir or pine; "holm" is the holm-oak, an evergreen oak.
Tine-tree is an old name for the laurustinus (Viburnum tinus), an evergreen shrub with dark blue berries.
The palm is called the reward of the conqueror because palm branches were given to victors in games and contests.
Attis, a youth loved by Cybele (Mother of the Gods), was turned into a pine after he was unfaithful to her; the story is only alluded to here.

context_notes.text: Orpheus, the legendary Thracian singer, was son of the Muse Calliope. His music could move animals, trees and stones, and he had just failed to retrieve Eurydice from the underworld.
Cybele, the Phrygian Mother of the Gods, was worshipped with frenzied rites by her eunuch priests, who were devoted to Attis; the pine was sacred to her.

literary_notes.text: The treeless hill is shaded only by song, so music alone creates the landscape; the shade, not the trees, is first to arrive.
The long list of trees displays Ovid's learning and shows the extent of Orpheus' power, as each species gathers one after another.
The sudden address "You, too, the ivy-trees" makes the narration vivid, as if the poet were watching the trees arrive.
